questions.questionText: You are deploying a new relational database using Cloud SQL. You are unsure exactly how fast the database will grow and want to avoid database downtime due to running out of disk space, without heavily over-provisioning storage upfront. Which feature should you enable?
options: Automatic storage increase
Cloud Storage bucket syncing
Compute Engine autoscaler
Dynamic persistent disk attachment
correctAnswers: Automatic storage increase

explanation.general explanation: Cloud SQL provides a feature called 'Automatic storage increase'. When enabled, Cloud SQL automatically checks the available storage every 30 seconds and automatically adds storage capacity if the instance is nearing its limit, preventing downtime without requiring manual intervention or massive upfront allocation.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage bucket syncing: Cloud Storage is object storage and cannot be used to dynamically extend the block storage capacity of a running Cloud SQL instance.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine autoscaler: The Compute Engine autoscaler adds or removes VM instances in an instance group; it does not allocate block storage to Cloud SQL.
why other options are wrong.Dynamic persistent disk attachment: You cannot manually attach arbitrary Compute Engine Persistent Disks to a managed Cloud SQL instance to expand its capacity.

questions.questionText: You have provisioned a 50 GB standard Persistent Disk (pd-standard) for your Compute Engine virtual machine. The application is experiencing high latency, and monitoring shows the disk has hit its maximum IOPS limit. What is the simplest way to allocate more IOPS to this specific disk type?
options: Increase the allocated capacity (size) of the Persistent Disk.
Enable the 'High IOPS' toggle in the Google Cloud Console.
Attach a Local SSD and stripe the data.
Change the VPC network tier to Premium.
correctAnswers: Increase the allocated capacity (size) of the Persistent Disk.

explanation.general explanation: In Google Cloud, the performance (IOPS and throughput) of standard, balanced, and ssd Persistent Disks scales linearly with the allocated capacity. To get more IOPS on a pd-standard disk, you simply allocate a larger disk size.

why other options are wrong.Enable the 'High IOPS' toggle in the Goo: There is no 'High IOPS' toggle for standard Persistent Disks.
While this would increase IOPS, it requires significant architectural changes and OS-level RAID configuration, making it far more complex than simply resizing the disk.
Network tiers affect internet egress routing, not the IOPS performance of an attached block storage disk.

questions.questionText: Your organization uses Cloud Spanner for a highly scalable inventory system. The database is approaching its maximum allocated storage capacity limit per node. How do you allocate more storage capacity to a Cloud Spanner instance?
options: Increase the number of compute nodes (or processing units) in the instance.
Enable automatic storage increase on the instance.
Attach an external Persistent Disk to the instance.
Change the instance storage type from HDD to SSD.
correctAnswers: Increase the number of compute nodes (or processing units) in the instance.

explanation.general explanation: In Cloud Spanner, compute and storage allocation are inherently linked. Each node provides a fixed maximum amount of storage (historically 2TB, now up to 4TB). To allocate more total storage capacity for the database, you must scale up by adding more compute nodes or processing units.

why other options are wrong.Enable automatic storage increase on the: Cloud Spanner does not have a separate 'automatic storage increase' feature for disks; you must add nodes, which can be done manually or via autoscaling configurations.
why other options are wrong.Attach an external Persistent Disk to th: Cloud Spanner is a fully managed service; you cannot attach raw Persistent Disks to it.
why other options are wrong.Change the instance storage type from HD: Cloud Spanner only uses SSDs; there is no HDD option, and changing types wouldn't increase capacity anyway.

questions.questionText: A junior developer accidentally allocated a 10 TB Persistent Disk for a small application that only requires 100 GB of storage. To optimize costs, you want to decrease the allocated size of this disk back to 100 GB. What is the correct procedure?
options: Create a new 100 GB disk, copy the data from the 10 TB disk to the new disk, and delete the 10 TB disk.
Use the Google Cloud Console to simply shrink the disk size to 100 GB online.
Use the `gcloud compute disks resize` command with the `--size=100GB` flag.
Unmount the disk from the VM, resize it to 100 GB in the console, and remount it.
correctAnswers: Create a new 100 GB disk, copy the data from the 10 TB disk to the new disk, and delete the 10 TB disk.

explanation.general explanation: In Google Cloud, you can only increase the size of a Persistent Disk; you cannot decrease (shrink) its allocated size. To reduce storage allocation, you must provision a new, smaller disk, manually migrate the data, and then delete the oversized disk.

why other options are wrong.Use the Google Cloud Console to simply s: The Google Cloud Console does not allow shrinking a Persistent Disk.
why other options are wrong.Use the `gcloud compute disks resize` co: The `gcloud` command will fail with an error if you attempt to specify a size smaller than the current allocated capacity.
why other options are wrong.Unmount the disk from the VM, resize it: Unmounting the disk does not bypass the fundamental restriction that Persistent Disks cannot be shrunk.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning a high-performance database on Compute Engine and need extremely low-latency, ephemeral local storage. You want to allocate exactly 1.5 TB of Local SSD capacity to the virtual machine. How is this capacity allocated?
options: By attaching four 375 GB Local SSD partitions to the virtual machine.
By creating a single Local SSD disk with a custom size of 1500 GB.
By selecting the 'pd-extreme' disk type and setting the size to 1.5 TB.
By enabling hyper-threading and allocating 1.5 TB of memory to a RAM disk.
correctAnswers: By attaching four 375 GB Local SSD partitions to the virtual machine.

explanation.general explanation: Local SSDs in Google Cloud are physically attached to the host server and are strictly allocated in fixed increments of 375 GB. To achieve 1.5 TB of Local SSD storage, you must attach exactly four 375 GB Local SSD partitions to the VM.

why other options are wrong.By creating a single Local SSD disk with: You cannot specify custom sizes for Local SSDs; they only come in 375 GB blocks.
why other options are wrong.By selecting the 'pd-extreme' disk type: pd-extreme is a network-attached Persistent Disk type, not a physically attached ephemeral Local SSD.
why other options are wrong.By enabling hyper-threading and allocati: A RAM disk uses system memory, which is highly expensive and completely different from allocating physical Local SSD NVMe drives.

questions.questionText: Your team wants to adopt an architecture where they never have to think about upfront disk sizing or capacity planning for their structured analytics and unstructured media files. Which two Google Cloud services are fully managed, do not require upfront storage capacity allocation, and simply charge for the data actually stored? (Choose two)
options: Cloud Storage
BigQuery
Cloud SQL
Compute Engine Persistent Disk
Filestore
correctAnswers: Cloud Storage
BigQuery

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Storage (for unstructured data) and BigQuery (for structured data analytics) are fully serverless storage solutions. You do not allocate disk size when creating a bucket or dataset; capacity grows seamlessly and infinitely, and you are billed only for the bytes actually consumed.

why other options are wrong.Cloud SQL: Requires you to provision an initial disk size, even if automatic storage increase is enabled.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Persistent Disk: Requires explicit allocation of block storage capacity in GBs or TBs at creation.
why other options are wrong.Filestore: Requires explicit capacity tier allocation (e.g., minimum 1 TB for Basic HDD) during instance creation.

questions.questionText: Your company uses Cloud Bigtable to store massive amounts of time-series IoT data. The operations team notices that the cluster is approaching 80% of its maximum storage capacity. How do you increase the total allocated storage limit of the Bigtable cluster?
options: Increase the number of nodes in the Bigtable cluster.
Resize the attached persistent disks in the Google Cloud Console.
Change the cluster storage type from SSD to HDD.
Enable the 'Auto-expand storage' flag in the Bigtable instance settings.
correctAnswers: Increase the number of nodes in the Bigtable cluster.

explanation.general explanation: In Cloud Bigtable, the maximum amount of data you can store is strictly proportional to the number of nodes in the cluster. Each node supports a specific maximum amount of storage (e.g., 2.5 TB for SSD, 8 TB for HDD). To allocate more total storage capacity, you must add more nodes.

why other options are wrong.Resize the attached persistent disks in: Bigtable does not expose underlying persistent disks for manual resizing.
why other options are wrong.Change the cluster storage type from SSD: You cannot change the storage type (SSD to HDD or vice versa) of an existing Bigtable cluster after it has been created.
why other options are wrong.Enable the 'Auto-expand storage' flag in: Bigtable does not have an 'Auto-expand storage' flag; capacity must be managed by scaling nodes (which can be automated via autoscaling, but fundamentally requires adding nodes).

questions.questionText: A media company is migrating to Google Cloud and plans to store approximately 50 TB of video files. The engineers are trying to figure out how to provision the Cloud Storage bucket to ensure it has exactly 50 TB of space allocated. What should you tell them?
options: Cloud Storage does not require upfront capacity allocation; it scales automatically as objects are added.
They must select the 'Enterprise' bucket tier to unlock capacities above 10 TB.
They need to pre-allocate 50 TB during bucket creation to guarantee availability.
They should create 10 buckets of 5 TB each to bypass the bucket size limits.
correctAnswers: Cloud Storage does not require upfront capacity allocation; it scales automatically as objects are added.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Storage is a fully managed object storage service that provides virtually infinite capacity. Users do not pre-allocate or provision a specific amount of storage (like GBs or TBs) when creating a bucket; they simply upload data and pay for what they use.

why other options are wrong.They must select the 'Enterprise' bucket: There is no 'Enterprise' tier for bucket capacity; all buckets scale infinitely.
why other options are wrong.They need to pre-allocate 50 TB during b: Pre-allocation is impossible and unnecessary in Cloud Storage.
why other options are wrong.They should create 10 buckets of 5 TB ea: There is no 5 TB bucket limit. A single bucket can easily hold petabytes of data.

questions.questionText: You are creating a Filestore instance to provide a fully managed NFS file share for your Compute Engine instances. You have selected the Basic HDD service tier. What is the minimum storage capacity you must allocate for this instance?
options: 1 TB
500 GB
2.5 TB
10 TB
correctAnswers: 1 TB

explanation.general explanation: Filestore has minimum capacity requirements depending on the selected tier. For the Basic HDD tier, the minimum provisioned capacity you can allocate is 1 TB.

why other options are wrong.500 GB: This is below the minimum allowed allocation for any Filestore tier.
why other options are wrong.2.5 TB: This is the minimum capacity allocation for the Basic SSD tier, not the Basic HDD tier.
why other options are wrong.10 TB: This is the minimum capacity allocation for the High Scale tier, not the Basic HDD tier.

questions.questionText: You need to increase the storage capacity of a Persistent Disk attached to a running Compute Engine virtual machine from 100 GB to 200 GB. Which two distinct operational steps are required to make this new space available to the application? (Choose two)
options: Increase the allocated size of the disk using the Google Cloud Console or CLI.
Resize the file system from within the guest operating system of the VM.
Stop the virtual machine before resizing the disk in the console.
Unmount the disk from the OS before applying the size increase.
Change the disk type to a higher capacity tier like pd-ssd.
correctAnswers: Increase the allocated size of the disk using the Google Cloud Console or CLI.
Resize the file system from within the guest operating system of the VM.

explanation.general explanation: Expanding a Persistent Disk is a two-step process. First, you allocate more underlying block storage capacity via the Google Cloud platform (Console, CLI, or API). Second, you must log into the guest OS and use system utilities (like `resize2fs` on Linux) to expand the file system so the OS can actually use the newly allocated space.

why other options are wrong.Stop the virtual machine before resizing: Persistent Disks can be resized online while attached to a running VM; stopping the VM is not required.
why other options are wrong.Unmount the disk from the OS before appl: You do not need to unmount the disk; online resizing is fully supported by modern operating systems.
why other options are wrong.Change the disk type to a higher capacit: Changing the disk type alters performance characteristics, but does not inherently increase the allocated size.

questions.questionText: You have enabled the 'Automatic storage increase' feature on your Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance to prevent out-of-disk outages. However, your finance team is concerned that a runaway script could fill the database with junk data, causing the storage allocation and monthly bill to grow infinitely. How can you mitigate this risk?
options: Configure a maximum storage limit in the Cloud SQL instance settings.
Set an overall billing quota limit on the Google Cloud project.
Attach a smaller Persistent Disk explicitly to cap the size.
Change the database instance to a read-only replica.
correctAnswers: Configure a maximum storage limit in the Cloud SQL instance settings.

explanation.general explanation: When you enable automatic storage increase in Cloud SQL, you can (and usually should) specify a 'maximum storage limit'. Once the allocated storage reaches this explicit limit, Cloud SQL will stop automatically adding space, preventing unbounded billing growth.

why other options are wrong.Set an overall billing quota limit on th: While you can set billing alerts, capping billing directly at the project level is complex and can shut down other unrelated services abruptly.
why other options are wrong.Attach a smaller Persistent Disk explici: Cloud SQL is a managed service; you cannot manually attach custom Persistent Disks to it.
why other options are wrong.Change the database instance to a read-o: Making the database read-only breaks the application's ability to function normally, rather than just preventing runaway storage growth.

questions.questionText: For standard Persistent Disks (pd-standard, pd-ssd), IOPS and throughput automatically scale with the allocated disk capacity (GB). However, you have a workload that requires extremely high IOPS but very little storage space. Which Compute Engine storage option allows you to provision and scale IOPS and throughput completely independently of the allocated disk size?
options: Hyperdisk (e.g., Hyperdisk Extreme)
Local SSD
pd-balanced
Regional Persistent Disk
correctAnswers: Hyperdisk (e.g., Hyperdisk Extreme)

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Hyperdisk is a next-generation block storage service that explicitly decouples performance from capacity. Unlike traditional Persistent Disks where IOPS are tied to disk size, Hyperdisk allows you to dynamically provision specific IOPS and throughput independently of the allocated GBs.

why other options are wrong.Local SSD: Local SSDs have fixed performance and size (375 GB increments); you cannot arbitrarily tune their IOPS independently.
why other options are wrong.pd-balanced: Performance on pd-balanced disks scales linearly with the allocated disk size.
why other options are wrong.Regional Persistent Disk: Regional PDs refer to replication across zones, but their performance is still tied to their allocated size.

questions.questionText: You have a 5 TB pd-ssd Persistent Disk attached to a VM. The data on it is only accessed for reporting during the last two days of the year. For the other 363 days, the VM is stopped, but you continue to pay high storage allocation costs for the 5 TB pd-ssd. What is the most cost-effective way to preserve this data while minimizing storage allocation costs?
options: Create a snapshot of the Persistent Disk, then delete the original disk.
Change the disk type from pd-ssd to pd-standard while the VM is stopped.
Move the data to a Local SSD and stop the VM.
Enable 'Archive Mode' on the Persistent Disk.
correctAnswers: Create a snapshot of the Persistent Disk, then delete the original disk.

explanation.general explanation: You pay for the allocated size of a Persistent Disk as long as it exists, regardless of whether the attached VM is stopped. To save costs for rarely accessed data, take a snapshot (which uses much cheaper Cloud Storage snapshot pricing and only bills for compressed, actual data) and delete the expensive block storage disk. You can restore the disk from the snapshot when needed.

why other options are wrong.Change the disk type from pd-ssd to pd-s: While cheaper than pd-ssd, keeping a 5 TB pd-standard disk sitting idle for a year is still vastly more expensive than a snapshot.
why other options are wrong.Move the data to a Local SSD and stop th: Data on a Local SSD is permanently lost if the VM is stopped or deleted.
why other options are wrong.Enable 'Archive Mode' on the Persistent: There is no 'Archive Mode' feature for block storage Persistent Disks.

questions.questionText: You are designing an architecture that uses Local SSDs for a high-performance, temporary caching layer on Compute Engine. Which two statements accurately describe the characteristics and allocation constraints of Local SSDs? (Choose two)
options: They are physically attached to the server hosting the VM instance.
Any data stored on them is permanently lost if the VM is stopped or deleted.
They can be easily detached from one VM and reattached to another.
They are allocated dynamically in custom sizes ranging from 10 GB to 1000 GB.
They automatically replicate data synchronously across multiple availability zones.
correctAnswers: They are physically attached to the server hosting the VM instance.
Any data stored on them is permanently lost if the VM is stopped or deleted.

explanation.general explanation: Local SSDs are physically attached to the exact hardware node where your VM runs, providing extremely low latency. Because they are tied to the physical hardware, they are ephemeral; if the VM is stopped, terminated, or migrated to another node, the data on the Local SSD is permanently lost.

why other options are wrong.They can be easily detached from one VM: Local SSDs cannot be detached or moved between VMs; they are physically bound to the host node.
why other options are wrong.They are allocated dynamically in custom: They are allocated strictly in fixed 375 GB increments.
why other options are wrong.They automatically replicate data synchr: They offer no redundancy or replication; they are strictly local to a single physical server.

questions.questionText: A critical Cloud Spanner instance has reached 100% of its storage capacity based on the number of allocated nodes. Monitoring alerts were ignored, and no additional nodes were provisioned. What is the immediate impact on the database?
options: The database will reject any new write requests.
The database will automatically double its node count to prevent an outage.
The database will silently overwrite the oldest data.
The database will automatically transition to a degraded HDD storage tier.
correctAnswers: The database will reject any new write requests.

explanation.general explanation: If a Cloud Spanner instance reaches its maximum storage limit based on its allocated nodes/processing units, it will protect the integrity of the existing data by rejecting any new write operations until more nodes are added to increase the storage capacity.

why other options are wrong.The database will automatically double i: Unless an external autoscaler is configured, Spanner does not automatically scale nodes by itself when full.
why other options are wrong.The database will silently overwrite the: Spanner is an ACID-compliant relational database; it never silently drops or overwrites data.
why other options are wrong.The database will automatically transiti: Spanner uses exclusively SSDs and does not migrate data to a lower tier when full.

questions.questionText: You run a large data purge on a 2 TB Cloud SQL instance, deleting 1 TB of old records. You now want to shrink the allocated storage of the Cloud SQL instance to 1 TB to reduce your monthly storage bill. How can you accomplish this?
options: You must export the data, create a new smaller Cloud SQL instance, and import the data.
You can shrink the disk size directly in the Cloud SQL settings via the console.
Cloud SQL will automatically shrink the allocated disk size during its next maintenance window.
Run the `VACUUM` command in the database, which triggers an automatic disk shrink.
correctAnswers: You must export the data, create a new smaller Cloud SQL instance, and import the data.

explanation.general explanation: In Google Cloud, block storage (Persistent Disks) underlying Cloud SQL instances can be increased but can never be decreased (shrunk). To reduce the allocated storage capacity and save money, you must export the database to Cloud Storage, provision a brand new, smaller Cloud SQL instance, and import the data.

why other options are wrong.You can shrink the disk size directly in: The console does not allow you to enter a smaller size for an existing disk.
why other options are wrong.Cloud SQL will automatically shrink the: Cloud SQL never automatically shrinks disks; it can only auto-increase them.
why other options are wrong.Run the `VACUUM` command in the database: Database vacuuming frees up space *inside* the database files for new rows, but it does not shrink the underlying allocated block storage disk.

questions.questionText: By default, BigQuery bills for storage allocation based on 'logical' uncompressed bytes. However, you can optionally switch the billing model to allocate costs based on 'physical' storage. Why would an organization choose to be billed based on physical storage allocation?
options: Their datasets contain highly compressible data, resulting in fewer physical bytes stored on disk.
Physical storage billing bypasses BigQuery query scanning costs.
Physical storage billing is required to use time travel and fail-safe features.
It allocates data to faster SSDs instead of standard HDDs.
correctAnswers: Their datasets contain highly compressible data, resulting in fewer physical bytes stored on disk.

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery physically compresses data under the hood. If your dataset contains highly compressible text or JSON data, the physical bytes written to disk will be much smaller than the raw logical bytes. Switching to physical storage billing can significantly reduce costs for highly compressible datasets (though physical billing includes time-travel bytes, so it requires careful evaluation).

why other options are wrong.Physical storage billing bypasses BigQue: Storage billing and compute/query billing are entirely separate in BigQuery.
why other options are wrong.Physical storage billing is required to: Time travel is available under both billing models (though physical billing charges for the time-travel storage explicitly).
why other options are wrong.It allocates data to faster SSDs instead: BigQuery storage infrastructure is managed by Google and is identical regardless of the billing model you choose.

questions.questionText: While Cloud Storage buckets have virtually unlimited overall capacity, there is a strict limit on the allocated size of a single uploaded object. What is the maximum size allowed for a single object in Cloud Storage?
options: 5 TB
1 TB
64 TB
100 GB
correctAnswers: 5 TB

explanation.general explanation: In Google Cloud Storage, while you can store an unlimited number of objects in a bucket, the absolute maximum allocated size for any single individual object (file) is 5 Terabytes (TB).

why other options are wrong.1 TB: This is incorrect; the limit is 5 TB.
why other options are wrong.64 TB: This is the maximum size limit for a single standard Compute Engine Persistent Disk, not a Cloud Storage object.
why other options are wrong.100 GB: This is far below the actual 5 TB limit.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a highly available relational database on Compute Engine. To protect against a complete zone failure, you need the underlying block storage to automatically replicate every write synchronously across two zones. Which disk type should you allocate?
options: Regional Persistent Disk
Multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket
Local SSD
Zonal Persistent Disk with scheduled snapshots
correctAnswers: Regional Persistent Disk

explanation.general explanation: A Regional Persistent Disk is specifically designed to provide high availability by synchronously replicating data across two distinct zones within the same region. If one zone goes down, a VM in the secondary zone can force-attach the disk and resume operations with zero data loss.

why other options are wrong.Multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket: Cloud Storage is object storage, not block storage required to run a relational database.
why other options are wrong.Local SSD: Local SSDs are strictly bound to a single physical host and offer no replication across zones.
why other options are wrong.Zonal Persistent Disk with scheduled sna: Snapshots are asynchronous and periodic; they do not provide real-time synchronous replication, meaning data created between snapshots would be lost in a zone failure.

questions.questionText: When allocating block storage for Compute Engine workloads, which two features are inherent to Regional Persistent Disks? (Choose two)
options: They synchronously replicate data across two zones in the same region.
They provide high availability and zero RPO in case of a single zone outage.
They can be synchronously replicated across two different regions globally.
They inherently offer significantly higher IOPS than ephemeral Local SSDs.
They automatically load balance read requests across multiple attached VMs.
correctAnswers: They synchronously replicate data across two zones in the same region.
They provide high availability and zero RPO in case of a single zone outage.

explanation.general explanation: Regional Persistent Disks provide Active-Active synchronous replication across two zones within a single region. Because every write is acknowledged in both zones before returning success, they provide zero Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and protect workloads from single-zone failures.

why other options are wrong.They can be synchronously replicated acr: Regional PDs only replicate across zones within the *same* region, not across different regions.
why other options are wrong.They inherently offer significantly high: Local SSDs physically attached to the host provide vastly higher IOPS and lower latency than any network-attached Persistent Disk.
why other options are wrong.They automatically load balance read req: A standard Regional PD is generally attached to a single VM at a time in read-write mode; it does not act as a load-balanced shared file system.

questions.questionText: What primarily determines the maximum storage capacity allocation for a Cloud Bigtable instance?
options: The number of nodes in the cluster multiplied by the storage limit per node.
The size of the Compute Engine Persistent Disk attached during creation.
The storage quota defined at the Google Cloud Project level.
The amount of data written; it is infinitely serverless and has no node dependency.
correctAnswers: The number of nodes in the cluster multiplied by the storage limit per node.

explanation.general explanation: In Cloud Bigtable, storage capacity is directly tied to compute capacity. The total storage you can allocate is strictly determined by multiplying the number of nodes in your cluster by the maximum storage allowed per node (e.g., 2.5 TB for SSD or 8 TB for HDD).

why other options are wrong.The size of the Compute Engine Persisten: You do not attach or manage raw Persistent Disks for Bigtable; storage is managed internally by the service based on node count.
why other options are wrong.The storage quota defined at the Google: While quotas exist, the architectural determinant of a specific cluster's capacity is its node count.
why other options are wrong.The amount of data written; it is infini: This describes Cloud Storage or Firestore, but Bigtable explicitly requires node provisioning for both compute and storage capacity.

questions.questionText: You are building a mobile application using Firestore as the backend database. You expect the database to start at 10 MB and potentially grow to 50 TB over two years. How should you allocate storage capacity in Firestore to accommodate this growth?
options: You do not need to pre-allocate storage; Firestore automatically scales storage to meet demand.
You must provision a 50 TB disk during initialization to ensure capacity is reserved.
You must start with 1 TB and manually increase the allocation limit as needed.
You must attach a Cloud Storage bucket as the backend storage layer.
correctAnswers: You do not need to pre-allocate storage; Firestore automatically scales storage to meet demand.

explanation.general explanation: Firestore is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL document database. It does not require any upfront storage provisioning or capacity allocation. It automatically scales to handle your data from megabytes to terabytes, and you are only billed for the storage you actually use.

why other options are wrong.You must provision a 50 TB disk during i: Firestore abstracts away all underlying disks; you cannot provision block storage for it.
why other options are wrong.You must start with 1 TB and manually in: There are no manual allocation limits or tiers to configure in Firestore for storage capacity.
why other options are wrong.You must attach a Cloud Storage bucket a: Firestore uses its own internal storage architecture; it does not rely on attaching Cloud Storage buckets for its primary database storage.

questions.questionText: Your production web server runs on Compute Engine with a 500 GB boot Persistent Disk. The disk is 95% full. You want to increase the allocated capacity to 1000 GB, but you cannot afford any downtime for the web server. Is this possible?
options: Yes, Persistent Disks can be resized online while the VM is running.
No, the VM must be shut down to modify the boot disk allocation.
No, boot disks cannot be resized; you must create a new VM from a snapshot.
Yes, but you must change the disk type to pd-extreme to support online resizing.
correctAnswers: Yes, Persistent Disks can be resized online while the VM is running.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud fully supports online resizing for Persistent Disks. You can increase the size of an attached disk (even the boot disk) without stopping or restarting the virtual machine, ensuring zero downtime for your applications.

why other options are wrong.No, the VM must be shut down to modify t: Stopping the VM is not required for resizing Persistent Disks.
why other options are wrong.No, boot disks cannot be resized; you mu: Boot disks can absolutely be resized dynamically.
why other options are wrong.Yes, but you must change the disk type t: Online resizing is supported across standard, balanced, and ssd Persistent Disk types.

questions.questionText: You previously allocated a 2 TB Filestore Basic tier instance for a shared team drive. The drive is nearly full, and the team needs an additional 2 TB of space. How should you expand the storage allocation?
options: Scale up the capacity of the existing Filestore instance dynamically.
Create a second 2 TB Filestore instance and mount it alongside the first.
Stop the Filestore instance, resize the disk, and restart it.
Filestore Basic tier cannot be expanded; you must upgrade to the Enterprise tier.
correctAnswers: Scale up the capacity of the existing Filestore instance dynamically.

explanation.general explanation: Filestore allows you to dynamically scale up the allocated capacity of an existing instance (for both Basic and other tiers) without requiring any downtime or interrupting active NFS connections.

why other options are wrong.Create a second 2 TB Filestore instance: While possible, this forces users to manage multiple network drives. Scaling the existing instance is the proper and simpler way to expand capacity.
why other options are wrong.Stop the Filestore instance, resize the: There is no need to stop the instance; capacity expansion is performed online.
why other options are wrong.Filestore Basic tier cannot be expanded;: The Basic tier fully supports dynamic capacity expansion.

questions.questionText: When allocating block storage for a high-performance database on Compute Engine, you want to ensure the underlying physical storage media is Solid State Drive (SSD) based. Which two Persistent Disk types provide SSD-backed storage? (Choose two)
options: pd-ssd
pd-balanced
pd-standard
Cloud Storage Nearline
Filestore Basic HDD
correctAnswers: pd-ssd
pd-balanced

explanation.general explanation: Both 'pd-ssd' (Performance SSD) and 'pd-balanced' (Balanced SSD) are Persistent Disk types backed by Solid State Drives (SSDs). pd-balanced provides a cost-effective middle ground between standard HDDs and high-performance pd-ssd.

why other options are wrong.pd-standard: pd-standard disks are backed by standard Hard Disk Drives (HDDs).
why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage Nearline: This is object storage, not block storage, and is intended for infrequently accessed data.
why other options are wrong.Filestore Basic HDD: This is a network file system explicitly backed by HDDs.

questions.questionText: You are allocating storage for a new Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. You must choose the underlying storage type. What are the two storage allocation options available for Cloud SQL instances?
options: SSD (Solid State Drive) and HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
Local SSD and Persistent Disk
Regional and Multi-regional
Hyperdisk Extreme and pd-balanced
correctAnswers: SSD (Solid State Drive) and HDD (Hard Disk Drive)

explanation.general explanation: When provisioning a Cloud SQL instance, you have two choices for the storage type: SSD (which is the default and recommended for most workloads) and HDD (which is cheaper and only appropriate for latency-insensitive or rarely accessed data).

why other options are wrong.Local SSD and Persistent Disk: Cloud SQL manages the disks internally using Persistent Disks; you do not choose between Local SSDs and PDs.
why other options are wrong.Regional and Multi-regional: These are location types for Cloud Storage, not storage types for Cloud SQL.
why other options are wrong.Hyperdisk Extreme and pd-balanced: These are specific block storage options for Compute Engine VMs, not the user-facing choices presented when configuring Cloud SQL.

questions.questionText: When you create a new bucket in Cloud Storage, you must specify how the data is geographically allocated. Which bucket property determines this and cannot be changed after the bucket is created?
options: Location Type (Region, Dual-region, or Multi-region)
Default Storage Class (Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive)
Object Lifecycle Management rules
Access Control (Uniform or Fine-grained)
correctAnswers: Location Type (Region, Dual-region, or Multi-region)

explanation.general explanation: The Location Type (whether the data is stored in a single Region, a Dual-region, or a Multi-region) fundamentally dictates where the physical data is allocated globally. Because this determines the underlying physical infrastructure, it is permanent and cannot be changed after the bucket is created.

why other options are wrong.Default Storage Class (Standard, Nearlin: You can change the default storage class of a bucket at any time.
why other options are wrong.Object Lifecycle Management rules: Lifecycle rules can be added, modified, or removed at any time.
why other options are wrong.Access Control (Uniform or Fine-grained): You can switch between Uniform and Fine-grained access control after bucket creation.

questions.questionText: While Firestore scales infinitely to handle massive databases, there is a hard storage allocation limit on the size of an individual document stored within the database. What is the maximum size of a single Firestore document?
options: 1 MB
10 MB
1 GB
100 KB
correctAnswers: 1 MB

explanation.general explanation: In Firestore, the maximum size for a single document (including all of its fields and data) is exactly 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes). If you need to store larger blobs, you should store the blob in Cloud Storage and keep a reference URL in the Firestore document.

why other options are wrong.10 MB: Incorrect; this exceeds the 1 MB limit.
why other options are wrong.1 GB: Incorrect; Firestore is not designed to store massive blobs inside a single NoSQL document.
why other options are wrong.100 KB: Incorrect; while good practice to keep documents small, the actual limit is higher (1 MB).

questions.questionText: You are migrating a massive legacy monolithic database to a single Compute Engine virtual machine. You need to attach the largest possible single standard Persistent Disk to the VM. What is the maximum allocated size for a single standard Persistent Disk?
options: 64 TB
10 TB
32 TB
100 TB
correctAnswers: 64 TB

explanation.general explanation: In Google Cloud Compute Engine, the maximum storage capacity you can allocate to a single, individual standard, balanced, or SSD Persistent Disk is 64 TB.

why other options are wrong.10 TB: This is incorrect; you can allocate much larger disks.
why other options are wrong.32 TB: This is incorrect; the limit is twice this amount.
why other options are wrong.100 TB: This exceeds the maximum allowed limit for a single Persistent Disk.

questions.questionText: Your Compute Engine application requires a small amount (2 GB) of ultra-fast 'scratch' storage. The data is entirely ephemeral and does not need to survive a reboot. You do not want to pay for a 375 GB Local SSD just for 2 GB of space. How can you allocate this ultra-fast ephemeral storage?
options: Mount a RAM disk (tmpfs) within the guest OS, which allocates storage from the VM's memory.
Allocate a 2 GB Local SSD in the Google Cloud Console.
Attach a 2 GB pd-extreme disk to the VM.
Use a Cloud Storage bucket mounted via Cloud Storage FUSE.
correctAnswers: Mount a RAM disk (tmpfs) within the guest OS, which allocates storage from the VM's memory.

explanation.general explanation: If you need a very small amount of extremely fast, ephemeral storage and don't want to use a full 375 GB Local SSD, the standard architectural approach is to mount a RAM disk (tmpfs in Linux) inside the OS. This allocates storage directly from the VM's available RAM, providing sub-millisecond latency for temporary files that are cleared upon reboot.

why other options are wrong.Allocate a 2 GB Local SSD in the Google: Local SSDs cannot be allocated in custom sizes; they are fixed at 375 GB.
Network-attached disks like pd-extreme will not match the latency of RAM, and using it for 2 GB of ephemeral scratch space is an anti-pattern.
why other options are wrong.Use a Cloud Storage bucket mounted via C: Cloud Storage FUSE provides high latency compared to local memory, making it completely unsuited for ultra-fast scratch space.
